A mortgage interest rate is the fee charged by a lender for borrowing money, expressed as a percentage. There are two basic types of mortgage rates: fixed and adjustable rates.

A fixed-rate mortgage locks in your rate for the entire life of your loan. For example, if you get a 30-year mortgage with a 6% interest rate, your rate will remain at 6% for the entire 30 years. (Unless you refinance or sell the home.)

An adjustable-rate mortgage keeps your rate the same for the first few years, then changes it periodically. Let's say you get a 5/1 ARM with an introductory rate of 6%. Your rate would be 6% for the first five years, and then the rate would increase or decrease once per year for the last 25 years of your term. Whether your rate goes up or down depends on several factors, such as the economy and the U.S. housing market.

At the beginning of your mortgage term, most of your monthly payment goes toward interest. As time passes, less of your payment goes toward interest, and more goes toward the mortgage principal or the amount you originally borrowed.

Two categories determine mortgage rates : those you can control and those you cannot.

What factors can you control? First, you can compare the best mortgage lenders to find the one that gives you the lowest rate and fees.

Second, lenders typically extend lower rates to people with higher credit scores, lower debt-to-income (DTI) ratios , and considerable down payments. If you can save more or pay down debt before securing a mortgage, a lender will probably give you a better interest rate.

What factors can you not control? In short, the economy.

The list of ways the economy impacts mortgage rates is long, but here are the basic details. If the economy — for example, employment rates — is struggling, mortgage rates decrease to encourage borrowing, which helps boost the economy. If the economy is strong, mortgage rates go up to temper spending.

With all other factors being equal, mortgage refinance rates are typically slightly higher than purchase rates. So don't be surprised if your refinance rate is higher than you may have expected.

30-year vs. 15-year fixed mortgage rates

Two of the most common mortgage terms are 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages . Both lock in your rate for the entire loan term.

A 30-year mortgage is popular because it has relatively low monthly payments. But it comes with a higher interest rate than shorter terms, and because you're accumulating interest for three decades, you'll pay a lot of interest in the long run.

A 15-year mortgage can be a good choice because it has a lower rate than you'll get with longer terms, so you'll pay less in interest over the years. You'll also pay off your mortgage much faster. But your monthly payments will be higher because you're paying off the same loan amount in half the time.

Basically, 30-year mortgages are more affordable from month to month, while 15-year mortgages are cheaper in the long run.

What bank is offering the lowest mortgage rates?

According to Yahoo Finance's Weekly survey of mortgage lenders with the lowest rates: A small turn lower , some of the banks with the lowest median mortgage rates are Chase and Citibank . However, it's a good idea to shop around for the best rate, not just with banks, but also with credit unions and companies specializing in mortgage lending.

Yes, 2.75% is an amazing mortgage rate. You're unlikely to get a 2.75% rate in today's market unless you take on an assumable mortgage from a seller who locked in this rate in 2020 or 2021, when rates were at all-time lows.

According to Freddie Mac, the lowest-ever 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 2.65%. This was the national average in January 2021. It is extremely unlikely that rates will dip below 3% again anytime soon .

At what rate should you refinance your mortgage?

Some experts say it's worth refinancing when you can lock in a rate that's 2% less than your current mortgage rate. Others say 1% is the magic number. It all depends on your financial goals when refinancing, how long you plan to stay in the same house, and on your break-even point after paying the refinance closing costs.

articles.title: High mortgage rates are deepening a ‘K-shaped’ housing market
articles.summary: In today’s housing market, there is a growing divide between the “haves” and the “have-nots.”
articles.body: In today’s housing market, there is a growing divide between the “haves” and the “have-nots.” The typical homebuyer faces mounting affordability challenges as home prices rise and inventory remains limited. Adding to the pressure: The recent surge in mortgage rates is making the decision to buy a home even more difficult for many, deepening affordability challenges The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.4% this week, according to data released Thursday by Freddie Mac. That’s a significant jump from this time last year, when the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.27%. With the US midterm elections just weeks away, rising mortgage rates are adding fresh pressure to an already strained housing market at a time when affordability issues are a key concern for many voters. Higher-income buyers, buoyed by more cash on hand and larger budgets, are accounting for a growing share of the housing market, while lower-income buyers struggle to keep up. It’s a divide that reflects the broader “K-shaped” economy: as the cost of living rises, wealthier Americans are better positioned to absorb the hit, while those with tighter budgets have less room to spare. The same split is playing out in the housing market: Americans who are less sensitive to higher interest rates increasingly have the upper hand. “It’s very expensive to get into a house if you’re looking for one right now,” said Oscar Munoz, head of US economics at TD Securities. “The only people that we find are driving transactions in the housing market are high-income consumers.” “They have the wealth to transact in this market, which is unaffordable for most Americans,” Munoz added. Data from TD Securities, commissioned by Morning Consult, shows a growing divergence in homebuying intentions this year. After tracking broadly with other income groups for several years, Americans earning $100,000 or more are now increasingly likely to say they want to buy a home, compared to lower-income consumers. The recent rise in mortgage rates above 7% may widen the gap, Munoz said, as higher monthly payments make it harder for lower-income Americans to qualify for a mortgage or afford the payments if they do. Higher-end buyers are likely also benefiting from a strong stock market, which hit record highs as recently as last week, giving them more purchasing power. “There are different markets by geography, different markets by price point. What we’re seeing is the low end is dragging down the overall market,” Compass CEO Robert Reffkin said of a slowdown in home sales in an appearance on CNBC last month. Rate-sensitive buyers getting spooked In Los Angeles, Brock and Lori Harris, a husband-and-wife real estate team, said buyers whose budgets are stretched by the prospect of higher mortgage payments have begun stepping back from the market. “I always find it funny that cars are marketed as a monthly payment, but homes are not. Homes just show the price and then you have to pull out your mortgage calculator to figure out what your payment is,” said Brock Harris. “And suddenly, that payment is much, much higher than it used to be.” National data points to a pullback from home shoppers who need to borrow money to afford a home. Mortgage applications last week were 16% lower than the same week one year ago, according to data the Mortgage Bankers Association released Wednesday. Brock and Lori Harris said they’re seeing more cash buyers in the market in LA, but even those buyers are keeping a tighter grip on their wallets than they did just a few years ago. “They’re aware, but they’re less sensitive to interest rates,” Lori Harris said of cash buyers. “Whereas a buyer who is taking out a loan might be priced out of a house they qualified to buy just two or three months ago because of these high rates.” Nationally, cash sales accounted for 27% of transactions in September, according to the National Association of Realtors’ latest data released Tuesday. That is down from 30% a year ago, but mortgage rates didn’t breach 7% until the final week of September, crossing a threshold that some experts say could make buyers who rely on mortgage loans hit pause. Mortgage rates tend to track bond yields, which have been volatile in recent months as investors anticipate further Federal Reserve rate hikes to rein in inflation. Those expectations have pushed bond yields higher, putting upward pressure on mortgage rates. In the weeks after mortgage rates crossed 7% late last month, eXp Realty, one of the country’s largest real estate brokerages, saw a higher-than-usual deal cancellation rate, said Leo Pareja, the CEO of AGNT, the parent company of eXp Realty. “What that tells us is that it is shocking psychologically. It’s a real barrier,” Pareja told CNN, though he added that the deal cancellation rate has since returned to normal levels for this time of year. For home shoppers still hunting for affordability in this higher interest rate environment, Pareja advised looking at new construction. New homes have traditionally commanded a price premium over existing homes, but that relationship has flipped over the past two years. Existing home prices rose 1.3% year over year in September to $417,500, marking 39 consecutive months of annual gains, according to NAR. Meanwhile, the median price of a new home was $393,700 in August, according to the latest Census Bureau data. “Unlike a homeowner who tests the market and doesn’t get their price, they can just pull it off the market if they have a lower interest rate… but a builder is in the business of selling,” Pareja said. As a result, builders are leaning more heavily on incentives to attract new buyers, including mortgage rate buydowns that can help lower monthly payments, Pareja said.

articles.title: AI trade rout sparks flight to Treasurys, bond yields sink: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: Investors flocked to safety as the AI trade has unwound over the past two sessions.
articles.body:
A sell-off in the AI trade has fueled investor interest in Treasurys, driving dramatic swings in bond yields.

The 10-year Treasury ( ^TNX ) yield, used as a benchmark for mortgages and other loans, sank 14 basis points to 5.05%. The 30-year yield (^ TYX ) also tumbled 13 basis points to 5.40%, as seen on Yahoo Finance's AlphaSpace chart below.

A global sell-off in chip stocks , exacerbated by AI financing worries , pushed investors toward Treasurys. Bond yields extended declines after reversing their gains on Wednesday following a hotter-than-expected inflation report.

The two-day action in bond yields could be a precursor to the road ahead if AI spending were to decelerate.

"It would weaken the USD and reduce US yields across the curve," wrote Thierry Wizman, global FX & rates strategist at Macquarie Group.

"That's because it would mark the end of superlative US growth against the rest of the developed economies," he said.

Bond yields have hit the highest levels in more than 20 years , raising concerns about higher borrowing costs and their impact on the broader stock market.

Sticky inflation has also led strategists to price in at least another rate hike this year. However, as of Thursday morning, market participants have raised their probability to 72% that Federal Reserve officials will hold rates steady at their policy meeting this month.

Macquarie Group strategists, along with UBS and Goldman Sachs analysts, see a Fed pause in October, followed by a rate hike at the Fed's December meeting.

articles.title: Rocket Lab stock tumbles as effort to take market share from SpaceX slips to 2027
articles.summary: Rocket Lab stock tumbled on Thursday after the space company said the first launch of Neutron, its reusable medium-lift rocket, slipped to 2027.
articles.body:
Rocket Lab ( RKLB ) stock tumbled more than 10% on Thursday after the space company said the first launch of Neutron, its reusable medium-lift rocket, slipped to 2027.

Rocket Lab had targeted the fourth quarter of 2026 for Neutron's debut. CEO Peter Beck blamed manufacturing issues in the forward propellant dome on the rocket's first stage.

"They don't necessarily mean that the dome would fail on flight, but our practice is to proceed only when we believe the system has the appropriate margins," Beck said in a video update, according to Stocktwits. "Possible success isn't our standard."

Beck said the company has identified manufacturing fixes and expects to finish assembling the first stage within the quarter, when it will be in a better position to announce a launch date. He also pointed to strong demand and upcoming contract announcements.

Neutron is central to Rocket Lab's effort to compete for larger missions in a market dominated by SpaceX's ( SPCX ) Falcon 9. Its schedule has slipped before: Rocket Lab unveiled the rocket in 2021 with a 2024 first-flight target, then moved it to mid-2025 and then to 2026. A first-stage tank ruptured during testing in January.

The plunge came after a 7.9% drop in Wednesday's regular session, before Rocket Lab released the update at 4:40 p.m. ET.

If Thursday's drop holds through the close, it would be Rocket Lab's lowest close since December 2025. The stock is down around 25% this year and about 65% below its 52-week high of $151, set in May.

Space stocks were already under pressure. AST SpaceMobile ( ASTS ) fell 10% Wednesday after Piper Sandler cut its price target to $54, citing competition from SpaceX.

Rocket Lab is also working to close its deal for satellite operator Iridium ( IRDM ).

Cantor Fitzgerald kept its Overweight rating and $122 price target on Rocket Lab after the update, according to Yahoo Finance analyst data.

articles.title: He bought a home, gave it for redevelopment years later and sold new flat for Rs 1.95 crore within 8 days; taxman denied LTCG exemption and added Rs 80.14 lakh, but ITAT grants relief
articles.summary: You buy a flat and after some years the housing society gives it for redevelopment.
articles.body: You buy a flat and after some years the housing society gives it for redevelopment. You then sell the redeveloped flat within days of getting it and claim long-term capital gains exemption.But the Income Tax Department treats these as two different transactions and applies short-term capital gains tax. What do you do?In one such case a man faced a tax notice and subsequently had to appeal before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), where he won relief.What the case is about The man had purchased a 510-square-foot flat in a housing society in Mumbai, during FY 2006-07, where he lived with his wife. Many years later, in FY 2012-13, the housing society entered into a redevelopment agreement with a builder. Under the arrangement, the man was allotted a replacement flat in the same society. This flat had 30% more area than his original home.Also Read | Man enters JDA for land, gets 6 flats from builder and transfers 5 to wife, but gets tax notice; ITAT Delhi deletes Rs 4.14 crore additions after finding no stock-in-trade conversion or saleThe builder handed over the redeveloped flat to the man after the two parties entered into an Agreement for Permanent Alternate Accommodation in 2018.However, eight days after signing the agreement, the man sold the redeveloped flat for Rs 1.95 crore.On his part, he classified the profit from this transaction as long-term capital gains (LTCG) and sought a tax exemption under Section 54F.The man said that he had invested the entire Rs 1.95 crore from the sale in purchasing another residential flat at a different location, making him eligible for the exemption.However, the Income Tax Assessing Officer (AO) took a different view. According to the AO, the transfer of the original flat to the developer under the redevelopment arrangement and the subsequent sale of the redeveloped flat were actually two separate transactions.With this view, the AO classified the gains as short-term capital gains (STCG), and denied the man the Section 54F exemption. This made the proceeds from the Rs 1.95 crore sale taxable. He also disallowed the benefit of indexation.The AO added Rs 80.14 lakh to the man’s taxable income, which was 50% share of the short-term capital gains.Also Read | Medicine shop owner deposited Rs 2.47 crore cash, faced unexplained money tax notice; ITAT Delhi says Income Tax Dept could not counter his evidence, rules in his favourThe Commissioner of Appeals also upheld the AO’s assessment. The appellate authority observed that the arrangement could not be treated as a straightforward sale and purchase.Instead, it involved the transfer of rights in the original flat, followed by the allotment of a newly constructed, substantially larger property under the redevelopment scheme.The man challenged the order before ITAT Mumbai. On July 16, 2026, the tribunal ruled in his favour.Why did the homeowner win the case?Chartered Accountant Suresh Surana told ET that ITAT Mumbai considered the redeveloped flat to be a continuation or substitution of the ownership rights associated with the original property.The tribunal held that such a property is not necessarily a new capital asset acquired only upon the execution of the Permanent Alternate Accommodation Agreement (PAAA).Under the redevelopment arrangement entered into by the housing society and accepted by the man, he was entitled to permanent alternate accommodation that included the area of his original flat, an additional 30% in carpet area at no cost, 185 square feet transferred by his mother and another 55 square feet purchased from the developer for Rs 6 lakh.The tribunal also ruled that the various portions of the redeveloped flat could not be treated as separate capital assets simply because the man received additional space or purchased extra area as part of the redevelopment arrangement.Also Read | Homebuyer paid Rs 91 lakh upfront for a Rs 1.24 crore property, but circle value rose to Rs 1.46 crore by registration; why ITAT Kolkata gave her tax relief and deleted Rs 11.35 lakh additionThe AO had accepted that Section 56(2)(x) did not apply to the transaction, since the man received the redeveloped flat under the redevelopment arrangement. The payment of Rs 6 lakh was considered to relate only to the additional area he had purchased.For calculating the capital gains, however, the AO treated the redeveloped flat as a separate asset acquired afresh on the date the Permanent Alternate Accommodation Agreement (PAAA) was signed. Since the man sold the property just eight days later, the resulting profit was classified as short-term capital gains (STCG).ITAT Mumbai rejected this interpretation, observing that redevelopment does not generally terminate an existing owner's property rights and replace them with ownership of an entirely new asset.Explaining the reasoning, Surana said: “Instead, the ownership rights continue throughout the redevelopment process and are substituted from the old premises to the newly constructed premises.”According to this interpretation, the PAAA only recorded and specified the permanent alternate accommodation that the taxpayer was already entitled to receive under the development agreement. It did not establish his ownership rights for the first time.Also Read |Man jointly bought Rs 80 lakh property with father and wife but didn't file ITR; taxman added Rs 55.2 lakh as unexplained money, but ITAT grants relief after proof of family contributionsSurana said: “Accordingly, the execution date of the PAAA could not be regarded as the starting point for computing the holding period.”The tribunal further clarified that the holding period must be calculated from the date on which the taxpayer acquired enforceable rights over the property, rather than the subsequent execution of the PAAA or a conveyance document. In this case, those rights originated in 2006 and remained in place throughout the redevelopment process.ITAT also considered an alternative calculation based on the development agreement dated February 15, 2013. Even if the holding period were counted from that date, the man had held the property for nearly five years before selling it on January 20, 2018. This was well beyond the prescribed 24-month period.ITAT Mumbai treated the gains of Rs 1.95 crore as long-term capital gains, allowed relief under Section 54/54F and set aside the Rs 80.14 lakh income tax addition.Also Read | Mother nominated son for savings account, but both died; Farmer father faced long delays, got money but lodged a compliant, Consumer Commission orders bank to pay Rs 15,000 reliefYou use AI every day. articles.summary: Tech stocks headed lower on Thursday as fears of debt financing swept through the AI trade.
articles.body: US stocks recovered on Thursday as Treasury yields tumbled and chip stocks pared losses following an AI-driven sell-off fueled by debt-financing concerns.The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) rose more than 400 points, 0.8%, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC) erased losses to hover near the flatline. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) fell 0.4% after declining more than 1% earlier in the session. A sell-off in tech over the past two days sparked a flight to treasuries with the 10-year bond yield (^TNX) sinking to 5.10%Semiconductor stocks trimmed earlier losses after the KOSPI index (^KS11) declined 7% overnight. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM) stock fell 2% on Thursday despite posting a record profit and beating estimates amid global demand for AI chips.Concerns over borrowing costs also weighed on the AI trade, hitting shares of Nvidia (NVDA)-backed CoreWeave (CRWV) after a 15% drop on Wednesday. The stock's sell-off underscored concerns about the neo-cloud provider's debt-heavy balance sheet and whether it can scale its business quickly enough to cover rising interest expenses.Meanwhile, new data showed September's wholesale inflation index rose at its fastest pace since 2022, sparking fresh concerns about how rising prices may affect the Federal Reserve's next move.
